<!-- paper:arxiv-2611-30284 -->
#### Interpreting the γ-Ray Emission of the Cygnus X region with a Combined Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3 Scenario

**Caijin Xie, Zhihao Ouyang, Yudong Cui and Lili Yang.** [arXiv:2611.30284v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30284v1) · [Full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30284v1). Submitted 23 November 2026, 08:40 UTC; new-primary entry in the 24 November UTC listing, astro-ph.HE. Preprint; no journal reference or acceptance recorded on the checked arXiv page.

**Question and approach.** Can one physically consistent superposition explain the Cygnus region from GeV to PeV energies, and can neutrinos distinguish hadronuclear from photohadronic emission? The paper combines the nearby Cygnus OB2 wind-termination shock, Galactic cosmic rays interacting with surrounding gas, and both compact and extended emission associated with the much more distant Cygnus X-3. These are sources projected onto the same sky region, not members of one physical association: the adopted distances are 1.46 and 9.0 kpc, respectively.

The calculation solves a steady, spherically symmetric diffusion–advection–loss equation for the proton distribution. OB2 has a termination-shock radius of 15 pc, a superbubble radius of 96 pc and a gas extent of 155 pc. The adopted effective gas density is 8.75 cm⁻³, after dilution of the molecular contribution. Inside the bubble the authors compare Kolmogorov, Kraichnan and Bohm transport; outside it they fix $D(E)=4.0\times10^{26}(E/\mathrm{GeV})^{1/3}\,\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}}$. The numerical calculation uses 1,000 spatial and 1,000 energy steps, with an iterated shock boundary condition. Gamma-ray production is computed with GAMERA, and photomeson production with the Hümmer et al. simplified interaction model; absorption on local stellar light and the cosmic microwave background is included.

**Results and assumptions.** In the tested wind-shock configurations, Kolmogorov and Kraichnan escape limit the high-energy output. Bohm transport with scattering-center drift parameter $\eta=0.11$ reproduces the spectrum below roughly 100 TeV but leaves a higher-energy deficit. Adding the Galactic cosmic-ray component helps without filling the PeV shortfall. A Cygnus X-3 core component fills the highest-energy end, while escaped protons supply the remaining several-hundred-TeV emission; in the resulting model Cygnus X-3 becomes dominant above about 200 TeV.

Two compact-source benchmarks fit the gamma-ray spectrum: $pp+p\gamma_{\rm UV}$ and $p\gamma_X+p\gamma_{\rm UV}$. Both fix the proton cutoff at 50 PeV. Their proton indices are 2.4 and 2.3 and their proton energies above 1 TeV are $6.6\times10^{39}$ and $4.8\times10^{39}$ erg, respectively, for a $10^{11}$ cm emission scale. The first uses a target density of $2.0\times10^{10}$ cm⁻³. The donor temperature is $3.75\times10^4$ K; the X-ray target is based on MAXI observations from 1 January 2020 to 1 January 2026. Extended emission uses an ambient density of 1 cm⁻³ and escape fractions of 0.009 or 0.005. These are adopted model parameters, not measured confidence intervals.

The predicted **single-flavor** core neutrino energy flux in the $pp+p\gamma_{\rm UV}$ case reaches approximately $E_\nu^2dN_\nu/dE_\nu\sim10^{-10}$ GeV cm⁻² s⁻¹ in the GeV band; the photohadronic alternative differs strongly there despite similar absorbed gamma-ray spectra. This is a discriminator proposed for future observations, not a neutrino detection.

**Limitations.** The spectral agreement is not a statistical rejection of every OB2 accelerator model. The calculation fixes simplified gas and transport geometries, assumes steady injection and a preserved escaping spectrum, and represents the average core flux as half its high-state value. The long-term duty cycle is therefore consequential. Its comparison of extended emission with a point-source IceCube limit and a projected NEON sensitivity is indicative; a spatially matched detector likelihood is needed for a detection forecast. Gamma-ray attenuation is included, but a self-consistent reprocessed electromagnetic cascade is not established here.

##### History

The extended-halo interpretation predates this paper. [Shi et al., arXiv:2607.07100](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07100) modeled continuous proton escape from Cygnus X-3 and compared both the spectrum and radial intensity above 400 TeV with LHAASO. Their benchmark fixes an injection index of 2, a 10 PeV cutoff and $D(1\,\mathrm{PeV})=3\times10^{29}$ cm² s⁻¹, with source ages of 100–400 kyr. With a vertically stratified gas distribution, the required cosmic-ray power was 1.6–3.2% of an assumed $5\times10^{39}$ erg s⁻¹ kinetic luminosity. Thus a distant microquasar halo was already an energetically plausible alternative to assigning all emission to the nearby stellar association. The present work adds an explicit OB2/Galactic-background/core/halo decomposition across a wider energy range and a low-energy neutrino comparison; it does not originate the microquasar-halo hypothesis.

An independent, relevant comparison is [Wan et al., arXiv:2610.11881](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11881), absent from the new paper's bibliography. That study jointly models the GeV and ultrahigh-energy spectra and orbital light curves, with anisotropic inverse-Compton emission and escaping protons interacting with stellar photons and competing disk/Wolf–Rayet winds. It finds that the gas encountered by the protons depends strongly on wind geometry, and that sustaining a dominant bubble contribution requires adequate time-averaged proton power or duty cycle. This exposes an important uncertainty in interpreting a successful steady spectral decomposition: compact-source high-state fits do not by themselves establish the long-term injection history of the extended halo.

<!-- paper:arxiv-2611-30661 -->
#### Reconstructing the depth of first interaction in extensive air showers from fluorescence detector profiles with a physics-motivated neural network

**Marcos Olegario and Vitor de Souza.** [arXiv:2611.30661v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30661v1) · [Full text](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30661v1). Submitted 23 November 2026, 13:21 UTC; new-primary entry in the 24 November UTC listing, astro-ph.HE. Preprint prepared for JCAP; no acceptance or journal publication was verified.

**Question and method.** Can fluorescence profiles recover the first-interaction depth $X_{\rm first}$, rather than only the shower maximum $X_{\max}$? For a fixed primary and energy, $X_{\rm first}$ follows an exponential distribution with interaction length $\lambda_{A\text{-air}}=\langle m_{\rm air}\rangle/\sigma_{A\text{-air}}$. Recovering its distribution would offer a route to hadronic cross sections and composition, although the first interaction itself usually produces too little fluorescence to observe directly.

The authors generate four million CONEX showers: proton and iron libraries for EPOS LHC-R and Sibyll 2.3d, spanning $10^{18}$–$10^{20}$ eV uniformly in log energy. They propagate fluorescence light through an atmosphere and an Auger-like detector response, including triggering, noise and reconstruction. Cuts require an observed track of at least 300 g cm⁻², a contained maximum and at least 200 g cm⁻² before it. A temporal convolutional encoder feeds a Gaisser–Hillas profile decoder and a second branch predicting seven ordered quantiles of $X_{\rm first}$. The profile-shape parameter $X_0$ is explicitly **not** identified with the physical first-interaction depth. Conditional distributions, rather than a histogram of point estimates alone, are used to reconstruct the population tail.

**Quantitative results.** In the $10^{19.0}$–$10^{19.2}$ eV bin, the mixed-model network obtains a proton mean absolute error of 20.78 g cm⁻² and correlation coefficient 0.752 with detector-level profiles, compared with 13.97 g cm⁻² and 0.872 for ideal profiles. Iron has a smaller absolute error, 6.75 g cm⁻², but a much weaker correlation, 0.398: its interaction length is itself only about 10 g cm⁻². Smaller absolute error therefore does not imply better physical reconstruction for iron.

Fitting the deepest 20% of the reconstructed distribution gives interaction lengths within 2% in same-model tests. With mixed-model training, the biases are +4.7% on EPOS LHC-R and −3.1% on Sibyll 2.3d; half their separation supplies the quoted approximately 4% **model-spread systematic**, not a confidence bound. Single-model cross-tests reach +8.4% or −6.0%. Raising iron contamination to 60% changes the reconstructed proton interaction length by less than 1%. Nominal 90% event intervals have 89.4–90.0% coverage in same-model tests, but cross-model coverage can fall to 86.7% for protons and 85.2% for iron.

**Limitations and interpretation.** This is a simulation-based method, not a new cross-section measurement. Training/test mixtures contain equal proton and iron fractions; helium and intermediate nuclei are absent. The weak dependence on iron contamination cannot be transferred to helium. Geometries are initially redrawn until every simulated shower passes selection, preserving the input depth distribution rather than reproducing an observed population. Reweighting by realistic selection changes the recovered interaction length by about −12% above $10^{18.6}$ eV. Requiring field-of-view coverage beyond 1,000 g cm⁻² and impact parameters below 15 km reduces that bias to about 1%, at a cost of a factor 2–4 in statistics; lower energies need further cuts. The approximately 4% uncertainty samples only two interaction models and is not a complete uncertainty budget for application to data.

##### History

The established observable is the exponential tail of $X_{\max}$, whose slope must be translated into a proton–air cross section using shower simulations. [The Pierre Auger Collaboration's 2012 analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.1520) measured $\sigma^{\rm prod}_{p\text{-air}}=505\pm22\,\mathrm{(stat)}^{+28}_{-36}\,\mathrm{(syst)}$ mb at a mean nucleon center-of-mass energy of 57 TeV, using $10^{18}$–$10^{18.5}$ eV events. It selected the deepest 20%, applied fiducial acceptance cuts and compared four hadronic generators; composition, especially helium, was a central uncertainty. That is an actual measurement. The new method aims to infer $X_{\rm first}$ more directly, but transfers part of the simulation dependence into the learned conditional distribution. Its simulation spread cannot be presented as an improvement factor over Auger's total measured uncertainty.

[Auger's average-profile measurement, arXiv:1811.04660](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04660), established that Gaisser–Hillas profiles describe measured averages to approximately 1% over −300 to +200 g cm⁻² around the maximum, while identifying atmospheric aerosols as an important shape uncertainty. This supports a physically structured decoder without guaranteeing faithful reconstruction of every individual shower. Independently, [Buitink et al., arXiv:2607.00135](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00135), not cited in the new paper, use simulated anomalous and double-bump showers to show how delayed energetic secondaries encode hadronic interactions beyond the first collision. Their proposed SKA-Low application concerns a different energy range and detector. Together these studies show why full profiles are informative, but also why a restricted smooth-profile model and uncertain early hadronic interactions remain important tests before deployment on data.

#### Search for Axion-like Particles using Blazar Observations with the HAWC Observatory

**R. Alfaro et al. (HAWC Collaboration).** [arXiv:2611.30818v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30818v1) · [Full text and complete author list](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30818v1). Submitted 23 November 2026, 15:09 UTC; new-primary entry in the 24 November UTC listing, astro-ph.HE. Preprint; the checked arXiv record gives no journal reference or acceptance.

**Question and data.** Photon–axion-like-particle conversion can let part of a gamma-ray beam cross intergalactic space without pair-production absorption, then regenerate photons in the Galactic magnetic field. Does the observed multi-TeV flux of distant blazars allow this extra transparency? The analysis combines approximately 3,000 days of HAWC Pass 5 observations from November 2014 to January 2024 with published H.E.S.S., MAGIC and VERITAS spectra for seven BL Lac objects at adopted redshifts 0.14–0.60. HAWC contributes a spatial Poisson likelihood with the full instrument response; the published IACT flux points enter a Gaussian likelihood. This is a constraint from existing observations, not a sensitivity forecast.

**Model and statistical treatment.** The interaction is $\mathcal L_{a\gamma}=-(g_{a\gamma}/4)aF_{\mu\nu}\widetilde F^{\mu\nu}$. Transfer matrices propagate an initially unpolarized photon beam through source jets, assigned intracluster fields, EBL attenuation and the regular Jansson–Farrar Galactic field. The baseline EBL is Domínguez et al.; intergalactic conversion is omitted. Intrinsic spectra are simple power laws: each source's normalization and slope are **profiled** independently at every mass–coupling point. Redshifts, source-field prescriptions and the absence of intrinsic spectral cutoffs are fixed assumptions, not parameters marginalized with broad priors. For PG 1553+113, the adopted redshift is 0.491 and the jet field is 0.5 G with Doppler factor 35.

For four cluster-associated sources the calculation uses 1,000 turbulent-field realizations, adopting the median survival probability and treating its 5th–95th percentile spread as a systematic variation; this is not a Bayesian marginalization over the full field likelihood. The exclusion scan covers masses 0.1–2,000 neV and couplings $10^{-12}$–$6\times10^{-11}$ GeV⁻¹ on a 25×25 grid. Two thousand pseudo-experiments calibrate each tested hypothesis, with spectral nuisance parameters refitted. Exclusion requires $CL_s<0.05$; a simple Wilks-theorem threshold is not assumed.

**Results.** No ALP signal is detected: the largest improvement has global $p=0.31$ after the scan. The lowest excluded coupling is $5.5\times10^{-12}$ GeV⁻¹ for masses below approximately 4 neV and reaches $4.6\times10^{-12}$ GeV⁻¹ around 6–9 neV. Exclusion extends to roughly 600 neV at larger couplings. Crucially, these numbers describe the **lower edge of a disconnected 95% $CL_s$ excluded set**. They do not exclude every larger coupling: below approximately 4 neV only 40% of scanned cells above that edge are excluded. The region becomes contiguous above its lower boundary for masses above roughly 50 neV within the scanned coupling range.

PG 1553+113 dominates: it excludes 178 of 625 tested cells alone, compared with 181 in the joint analysis. Changes of EBL prescription alter the excluded logarithmic parameter-space area by −36.5% to +32.6%; these are area changes, not percentage errors on $g_{a\gamma}$. Tested Galactic-field variants reduce the area by up to 15.5%, with smaller detector-response effects.

**Limitations.** The result depends on extrapolating the IACT-constrained intrinsic power laws into the strongly absorbed multi-TeV band. Intrinsic curvature or cutoffs can mimic a change in transmission. Noncontemporaneous source variability, approximate IACT energy dispersion and the neglect of correlations between published flux points are additional qualifications. Assigned source/cluster fields and a restricted family of Galactic-field alternatives do not span all astrophysical uncertainties. The dominance of one source further limits the interpretation of this as seven independent confirmations.

##### History

[Jacobsen, Linden and Freese, arXiv:2203.04332](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04332), already used the same seven nonflaring blazars to test enhanced TeV transparency. Their analysis combined IACT spectra with catalog-level HAWC information near 7 TeV and reported exclusions at greater than 3σ around $g_{a\gamma}\gtrsim3\times10^{-11}$ GeV⁻¹ for masses below roughly 200–300 neV. The new work replaces that compressed flux treatment with more exposure, improved event separation and the forward-folded count likelihood. However, it also changes statistical calibration, confidence convention and the definition of the excluded set. A ratio of the two lower-edge couplings is therefore not a like-for-like sensitivity improvement and is not quoted here.

The strongest relevant comparison at the lower masses is not only the earlier HAWC result. [Guo et al., arXiv:2507.07786](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07786), a primary study absent from the new bibliography, analyzed 16.5 years of Fermi-LAT observations of NGC 1275 between 100 MeV and 500 GeV. It reported a 95% exclusion reaching approximately $3\times10^{-12}$ GeV⁻¹ over 0.4–5 neV under a 10 μG central Perseus-field model, Domínguez EBL and Jansson12 Galactic field. It refits log-parabola normalization, index and curvature, fixes its spectral scale, and uses the fifth percentile of fitted χ² across 100 turbulent realizations with a Monte Carlo-calibrated threshold. Thus the new HAWC lower edge is not universally the tightest constraint at overlapping masses; its value is complementary energy and propagation coverage with different systematics. The much smaller couplings discussed for VLAST in that earlier paper are forecasts and are not existing exclusions.
